newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sues New York Blood Center.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sues New York Blood Center.

text.p: The federal government on Monday sued the New York Blood Center, the nation's biggest independent supplier of blood, for failing to maintain adequate methods of screening blood for infection.

Federal prosecutors simultaneously announced they had also filed a consent decree in which the center agreed to correct violations and take steps to assure the purity and quality of its blood products.

The center provides 80 percent of the blood supply in the New York area. It also provides blood donor testing services for facilities located in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Tennessee and imports and exports blood products to and from Europe.
The lawsuit, filed in Manhattan federal court, accused the blood center of violating the U.S. Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act.

The lawsuit provided a long list of violations including that the center did not follow standards designed to prevent the introduction, transmission or spread of communicable diseases including the HIV virus that causes AIDS.

The complaint named John Adamson, president and chief executive officer, as defendant, as well as Celso Bianco, vice president of medical affairs, and Jenni Lee Robins, vice president of blood operations.

In November, New York magazine ran a cover story reporting the federal probe and published allegations from employees that workers at the center had deliberately altered test restuls to allow more blood to be approved.
The FDA, which conducted inspections in 1994 and 1995 of NYBC's two locations in Manhattan, raised questions about the tests it used to screen blood.

It found that the center used improper testing practices, failed to maintain complete and adequate operating procedures; maintained inaccurate recordkeeping, provided inadequate personnel training and had inadequate security controls of computerized operations to ensure the integrity of the data.

The FDA notified the NYBC of its findings and issued a warning letter in March 1995. Prosecutors said the FDA is conducting an inspection and investigation which disclosed continuing violations of the blood safety laws and regulations.
